case_name: Nageshwar Prasad and Others v Union of India and Others
facts: Nageshwar Prasad and Others v Union of India and Others
Supreme Court of India, 28 July 1994, C.As.
The Order of the Court was as follows:
1. In exercise of powers conferred by the proviso to Art. 309 of the Constitution the President made Rules to amend the Central Water Engineering (Group B) Service Rules, 1964;
2. The promotion was to be effected by selection on the basis of merit with due regard to seniority from amongst persons employed in the Central Water Commission in the grades of;

3. The amended Rule provides that 50 per cent of the posts shall be filled by promotion of officers mentioned in sub-rule (1) possessing a degree in Engineering from a recognised University/Institution or equivalent and having rendered not less than three years' regular service in the respective grade in the capacity of a graduate engineer;

4. The history of this service shows that earlier under the Central Water Engineering (Class II) Service Rules, 1964 the quote prescribed was 66 2/3 for degree-holders and 33 1/3 for diploma-holders, vide Rule 13.

5. The diploma-holders are recruited in big numbers in the group C category below Assistant Engineers and since the sanctioned posts in the immediately next higher category of Assistant Engineers are limited in number, a large number of them stagnate and do not get even a single promotion.
6. Dealing with this challenge the Tribunal proceeded to answer the same as under;
7. After considering the various decisions of the Supreme Court, the Principal Bench held as follows;
8. It is thus obvious that while the difference in the experience criteria was upheld by the Tribunal it struck down the quota rule which limited promotion to 50 per cent for diploma-holders.

9. The learned counsel for the appellants contended before us that the question is squarely covered by three decisions of this Court reported in Roop Chand Adlakha v. DDA 1988 Indlaw SC 234, Govt. of A.P. v. P. Dilip Kumar 1993 Indlaw SC 935 and P. Murugesan v. State of T.N. 1993 Indlaw SC 937.

10. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the decisions on which the learned counsel for the appellants placed reliance cannot be distinguished on the observations made in Shujat Ali case 1974 Indlaw SC 5, to which our attention was drawn by the learned counsel for the diploma-holders as those very observations were explained in Roop Chand case 1988 Indlaw SC 234 and in Murugesan case 1993 Indlaw SC 937.
11. We are also not impressed by the submission that 50 per cent quota rule is violative of Articles 14/16 of the Constitution.

12. We, therefore, agree with the submission of the learned counsel for the appellants that the impugned decision of the Tribunal striking down the 50 per cent quota rule is clearly inconsistent with the ratio of the three decisions of this Court on which counsel for the appellants placed reliance.

13. Before we part we must, however, observe that if the contention of the learned counsel for the diploma-holders that there is large-scale stagnation and the majority of the diploma-holders have to retire without securing a single promotion in their entire service career is correct, the authorities concerned should look into the matter and redress their grievance in this behalf.
14. The appeals are accordingly allowed and shall stand disposed of with no order as to costs.
issues: The prescription of different periods of experience for degree-holders and diploma-holders
The prescription of the quote rule limiting promotion to 50 per cent for diploma-holders
petitioner_arguments: The question is squarely covered by three decisions of this Court reported in Roop Chand Adlakha v. DDA 1988 Indlaw SC 234, Govt. of A.P. v. P. Dilip Kumar 1993 Indlaw SC 935 and P. Murugesan v. State of T.N. 1993 Indlaw SC 937.

The decisions on which the learned counsel for the appellants placed reliance cannot be distinguished on the observations made in Shujat Ali case 1974 Indlaw SC 5, to which our attention was drawn by the learned counsel for the diploma-holders as those very observations were explained in Roop Chand case 1988 Indlaw SC 234 and in Murugesan case 1993 Indlaw SC 937.
respondent_arguments: The contention of the learned counsel for the diploma-holders that there is large-scale stagnation and the majority of the diploma-holders have to retire without securing a single promotion in their entire service career
The prescription of the quote rule is violative of Articles 14/16 of the Constitution
court_reasoning: The prescription of the quote rule is obviously to ensure that in the immediate promotion cadre there is a fair mix of both degree-holders and diploma-holders because the vertical movement from that stage and upwards in the hierarchy is restricted to degree-holders and if they are not available in sufficient number in the feeding channel the said channel would be virtually dry and sufficient number of degree-holders would not be available for promotion to the next higher cadre.
We, therefore, do not see how prescription of the 50 per cent quota is in any manner arbitrary.
holding: The appeals are accordingly allowed and shall stand disposed of with no order as to costs.
